articles.title: How Skyrim Found a Second Life As Cozy Game
articles.description: 15 years after release, Skyrim's icy, dangerous world feels warm and cozy. But why has this dark fantasy become such a comfort play? We spoke to experts and developers to find out.
articles.content:
Every few months, some YouTube channel will upload a video essay asking why we continue to play Skyrim more than a decade after release. Virtually all of them come to the same conclusion: at this point, what keeps us coming back for more isn’t the gameplay, or the story, or the seemingly never-ending wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, but the coziness of its setting.

At a glance, this makes perfect sense. After all, many of us no longer play Skyrim to progress the narrative or complete quests, but simply to spend time in its world. And yet, if you really think about it, it’s also kind of strange. Many cozy games are devoid of danger or pressure, and sport a warm, colorful, often cartoonish look. Skyrim, on the other hand, is dark fantasy 101, its lands frozen over and filled with scary, pointy things that can and will kill you if given the chance.

Sure, some use mods that remove enemies, shake up mechanics, and even clear up the weather, making the game look and feel more similar to cozy favorites like Animal Crossing or Stardew Valley. However, I don’t think I’m alone when I say that – to me – the base game already feels incredibly cozy as it is, dragons and all. For many years I’ve wondered why. And this month, in honor of Skyrim’s 15th anniversary, I took a stab at finding answers.

While researching, it quickly became clear that most of the common reasons for Skyrim’s coziness do not hold up to scrutiny. Yes, the game’s awe-inspiring landscapes and Jeremy Soule’s soundtrack definitely play a role, but I believe it’s only a supporting one. Otherwise, why would I feel a similar kind of coziness playing games like Bioshock or Batman: Arkham City, which look and sound completely different?

“Nostalgia,” you might say, and many do. But that doesn’t quite cut it either. While the world of Skyrim has indeed become like an old friend, and booting up the game reminds me of the carefree teenage years that coincided with my initial playthrough, the coziness I feel today is – for the most part – the same coziness I remember feeling back then.

The nostalgia factor connects to another, and in my opinion equally insufficient explanation: player competence. The more we play a game, the better we get, and the easier, less threatening, and therefore cozier said game should become. Again, not my experience. For me, playing with a heavily underleveled character, so that even the most ordinary enemy encounter becomes an existential threat, actually makes the game feel more cozy, not less. Strange right?

Danger and coziness don’t necessarily cancel each other out; designers can in fact use one to amplify the other. Not really, it turns out. While early reports on the design of cozy games connected coziness to an absence of danger, today we understand the relationship to be a bit more complicated. In an article about the rise of “dark” cozy games like Dredge and Cult of the Lamb, which play around with mechanics that scare, stress, or unsettle, Polish media scholar Agata Waszkiewicz argued that danger and coziness don’t necessarily cancel each other out. Quite the contrary, designers can in fact use one to amplify the other.

“Coziness is a tricky concept to define,” Waszkiewicz tells IGN, “so we often do it by juxtaposing it with something that clearly is not cozy. There’s a reason everyone always talks about being wrapped up in a blanket, drinking tea or hot cocoa, while it is pouring outside. That contrast between outside and inside makes coziness more pronounced and easier to grasp.”

“A cabin feels warm because of the blizzard,” agrees Rachel Kowert, a research psychologist who specializes in games and mental health. The psychology of cozy games make her think of something called Prospect-Refuge theory, which basically argues that people are evolutionarily “drawn to spaces where we can see out over the world while also being sheltered from it.”

FromSoftware games have clear equivalents of prospect-refuge points in the forms of bonfires, lamps, and sites of grace: locations that shield players from enemies, even when they’re standing right beside you, while also allowing you to level up, replenish resources, and prepare for the journey ahead. Our prehistoric ancestors would have surely been able to relate.

Skyrim may not have bonfires, but its world likewise contains plenty of places where players are in proximity to yet safe from threats. Think of when you’re passing over one of the province’s many mountaintops and see a dragon flying overhead, or a giant herding his mammoths down below. For me, these are precisely the moments when the game’s world strikes me as most peaceful, and Soule’s soundtrack most relaxing.

Mark Teare, an effects artist who has since left Bethesda and is now working on a cozy game of his own, can think of another reason for why Skyrim evokes such strong feelings of coziness in players: ants. Yes, there are ants in this game, and Teare is the one who put them there, despite Bethesda’s initial protests.

“My boss saw them and was like, ‘No one is ever going to see them. Why are we wasting time on this?’” he tells IGN. “But for me they were a big deal, precisely because they were so small. Once you notice them, the world just feels so much bigger. You wonder: how many other things am I walking by and not even seeing?”

These little details didn’t need to be there, but their presence shows players that we cared, and they feel that. This rationale touches on a number of things that are integral to cozy game design, including presence and connection. Cozy games often encourage players to slow down and appreciate things that in other types of games they might overlook or take for granted. Details like Teare’s insects also create a sense of intimacy. Not with other players, but with the developers: “These little details didn’t need to be there, but their presence shows players that we cared, and they feel that.”

Soule once said a very similar thing, stating in an old interview that he wanted the game’s music to be a constant companion. His goal wasn’t to feed into the game’s power fantasy, but make the player “not feel alone” and “like there’s meaning to what they’re doing.” Whether you’re an expert on Elder Scrolls lore or not, his ethereal soundtrack gives you a sense that some or other god is watching over you, and that – despite the chaos of civil war and the coming of Alduin – everything in this world is fundamentally in harmony.

Speaking to Teare, I stumbled upon my third and perhaps most compelling explanation for Skyrim ’s coziness: the fact that Bethesda didn’t intend for the game to feel cozy at all. “I was down in the trenches, so I’m not sure what the big, big plans were,” he says, “but I don’t remember any discussion or mandate or anything, and none of us were actively thinking about coziness while working.”

During our conversation, Teare brought up ASMR – a sensation closely related to coziness, and hugely influential to his ongoing projects. While there are lots of successful ASMR content creators out there, many aficionados will tell you that the most potent ASMR is created unintentionally. “When someone is trying hard, it feels manufactured,” says Teare. In his opinion, the best “ASMRtists” are “really good actors” that make what they’re doing seem natural even though it’s not.

You could make a similar argument about coziness, and I think mine is pretty solid. Research on cozy game design often mentions words like the Danish hygge and Dutch gezelligheid, both of which are frequently translated into English as coziness. As a Dutch person, I can say with authority that gezelligheid isn’t something you can just force into existence. Like at a great party where everyone gets along with everyone, true gezelligheid happens when the stars align, and everything feels alright in the world – all without you having to do anything…kind of like when you’re playing Skyrim, right?

As Waszkiewicz said, coziness is tricky to define. Not only because what constitutes as cozy differs from person to person, but also because no two games are cozy in the exact same way. I’m not trying to have the final word on this subject. My only goal was to try to articulate what makes Skyrim cozy to me, and what sets this coziness apart from other games. If you feel differently, let me know in the comments. I’d love to hear.

Tim Brinkhof is a freelance writer specializing in art and history. After studying journalism at NYU, he has gone on to write for Vox, Vulture, Slate, Polygon, GQ, Esquire and more.

articles.title: Anorak secures $5M to let anyone create their own AI-powered games
articles.description: Anorak, a London-Chengdu entertainment tech company with the vision of “making any pursuit playable”, today announced a $5 million pre-seed round co-led by Play Ventures and Backed VC, with participat...
articles.content:
Anorak, a London-Chengdu entertainment tech company with the vision of “making any pursuit playable”, today announced a $5 million pre-seed round co-led by Play Ventures and Backed VC, with participation from Supercell and MTG.

Anorak is led by CEO Shaun Rutland, who co-founded Hutch – the mobile automotive games studio behind Top Drives and F1 Clash, acquired by MTG in 2020 – and Chief Creative Officer Jonathan Alpine, a founding employee at Hutch and its former Chief Creative Officer.  They are joined by co-founder Tak Fung, Chief of AI, who leads Anorak's AI lab in Chengdu, China.

The company, which began as a generative video research project, now has a 20-strong team across London and Chengdu, developing proprietary inference technology to make generative video faster, cheaper and more controllable, progressively enabling games and experiences to shift from pre-generated to generative, real-time interaction.

The company's medium is interactive generative video – generative video, made playable. Rather than simply prompting its way to new AI-bolstered versions of existing games, Anorak is building new play patterns from scratch, and the platform to go with them. It’s a platform where generated video responds to user choices and inputs in real time. The model pairs human creativity and playfulness with agentic ingenuity and visualisation to establish an entirely new entertainment medium; one that is playable, watchable, and shareable.

At Hutch, the team learned how deep a single subculture can run. Car enthusiasts didn't just play – they obsessed over details, built communities and held each game to their own standards. Anorak takes that lesson and applies it to every subculture there is: anglers, sneakerheads, padel players, birdwatchers, K-pop fans, and thousands of communities no publisher would ever greenlight a game for. 

Generative media changes the economics of serving these communities. Anorak will bring its interactive format to increasingly wider and specific interests, making entertainment viable for audiences that traditional game production economics have left underserved.

The aim is to hand those tools to real-world communities, so they can make playable content for themselves – shaped by their own in-jokes, rituals and taste, not a boardroom's guess at what a mass market wants. When anyone can make anything, Anorak believes taste becomes the scarce asset, and the communities that hold it should not only steer what is created, but become the creators.

Anorak is releasing new playable experiments on its blog  every week, with plans to launch a creator platform that will enable anyone to realise their ideas.

It won't be a traditional chatbot that turns a prompt into a game. Anorak believes creation should be as much fun as playing – it's about having fun making fun.

According to Shaun Rutland, CEO and co-founder, Anorak:

"Every time making got cheaper – in music, film and games – value moved to whoever had the taste to filter the flood. Generative is the biggest of those shifts yet, because almost anyone can now create. 
Anorak is about giving every community that power: real people making playable things for the people they actually care about."

According to Harri Manninen, Founding Partner, Play Ventures, Anorak is at the forefront of building a new form of interactive entertainment, turning generative video into experiences people can play, watch and share. 

“What makes the vision especially compelling is the opportunity not only to build for passionate communities, but to empower those communities to create entertainment around their own interests. 

Shaun, Jonathan and Tak combine a proven track record in entertainment with deep AI expertise, exactly the kind of team we want to back at the beginning of a new technology cycle.”

Alex Brunicki, Founding Partner, Backed VC, contends that most AI entertainment companies are using new tools to make old formats faster. 

“Anorak is asking a far more interesting question: what does entertainment look like when content is made by and for a community, especially if we shift away from the skeuomorphism that other companies are still approaching the space with?

Furthermore, the technical breakthroughs the team have made in the past 12 months make us extremely excited for what comes next with Anorak."

The funding will expand the London and Chengdu teams, bring the first playable formats to release, and establish the creator platform in early 2027.

articles.title: Tekken Legend Katsuhiro Harada Says He Wishes 'Hardware Like the Xbox Series S Wouldn't Be Released'
articles.description: Tekken development legend Katsuhiro Harada had some strong comments for Microsoft's lower-powered Xbox Series S console, dubbing it a "weaker child" with "awkwardly lower performance."
articles.content:
Tekken development legend Katsuhiro Harada had some strong comments for Microsoft's lower-powered Xbox Series S console, dubbing it a "weaker child" with "awkwardly lower performance."

A number of video game developers have struggled with the Xbox Series S while following Microsoft's feature parity rules across Xbox Series consoles. Baldur's Gate 3 famously came to Xbox a few months late and required the help of Microsoft's engineers to get the game's split-screen co-op working on Series S. More recently, the developer of breakout shooter Wardogs admitted that the limitations of the Xbox Series S had stopped it from adding certain things to the game.

Indeed, one of the questions facing Microsoft ever since the release of the Xbox Series S back in 2020 is whether it would be willing to allow developers and publishers to release a game on Xbox Series X only, leaving Xbox Series S behind. As it stands, Xbox mandates that video games launch on both or none at all, and that there should be main feature parity between each version.

In a roundtable discussion held at the Console Game Developers Conference in Korea, Harada slammed the Series S and attempted to encourage Cyberpunk 2077 associate game director Paweł Sasko to join in the pile-on, too.

"There's something I really want to say while I have the floor," Harada began (thanks, Inven Global ), "since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released (laughs)."

Throughout his years in charge of Tekken, Harada has become known as a colorful character happy to express his opinions freely. And, to be fair, it sounds like Harada made the comment knowing he was being rather cheeky. But the developer then continued to explain his position further — and have Sasko back him up, following reports that CD Projekt struggled with Cyberpunk 2077's Series S version.

"I want to ask director Paweł personally," Harada continued. "Honestly, weren't you upset inside because of Series S?"

"It constantly throws challenges at us and forces us to optimize our code very cleanly," Sasko responded, appearing to tiptoe around the subject.

"You just used a very polite and elegant way to say 'Xbox Series S sucks,' right?" Harada ploughed on. "Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance. When porting to Switch 2, developers can shift their mindset to 'Switch 2 is a distinct device for Nintendo fans!' But with Xbox, after delivering your absolute best output, it feels like having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child."

Gosh. Tell us what you really think, Harada!

"Furthermore," he continued further, "in markets like the U.S., there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking 'Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?'"

While Harada's comments will likely not come as a shock to many developers who have been tasked with releasing games across the Xbox Series family this generation, it is rare to hear someone of Harada's prominence discussing the Series S' drawbacks out loud.

In response — and in a continued attempt to not say anything that would get him in trouble — Sasko acknowledged that such Series S drawbacks were real, but that the console also offered a lot of positives. Its more affordable price point meant that developers could get their games played by a wider audience, Sasko offered, while opimtization breakthroughs initially made for Series S had also benefited Cyberpunk 2077 across all platforms.

Acknowledging Sasko's more positive take, Harada concluded that he was now worried Microsoft would "feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

Will Xbox release a lower-powered Helix console? It's unclear. After earlier reports that suggested the new console was reportedly targeting a holiday 2027 launch, more recent estimates have pointed to a 2028 launch for the machine — at an eyewatering $1,200 - $1,800 price point. Maybe that will make Harada reconsider?

articles.title: SpaceX develops its own ‘Kessel’ rack-scale system featuring 72 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for data centers in space, report claims
articles.description: SpaceX is reportedly developing a 'Kessel' rack-scale system design with 72 Nvidia Rubin GPUs that relies on a massive 84-layer PCB midplane.
articles.content:
SpaceX/xAI is developing a custom version of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale AI system that replaces conventional NVLink cable assemblies with a massive 84-layer printed circuit board (PCB), in part for use in orbital data centers, reports SemiAnalysis. The system is codenamed Kessel and retains 36 Vera CPUs, 72 Rubin GPUs, and nine NVLink switch trays, but introduces a different solid-state interconnect architecture. While SpaceX/xAI will continue to buy Nvidia hardware directly from the company, Elon Musk's company will source other components independently, which could give it greater control over its hardware supply chain.

The Kessel system retains the fundamental configuration of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, which comprises 72 GPU packages distributed across 18 compute trays and nine NVLink switch trays. However, instead of Nvidia's conventional arrangement with internal NVLink cable cartridges, SpaceX plans to position compute and switch trays back-to-back around a passive PCB midplane. The architecture resembles a smaller version of Nvidia's Kyber design with 576 AI GPUs (albeit in 144 packages), which also relies on a PCB-based interconnect rather than conventional cable assemblies, SemiAnalysis notes. Interestingly, the design is aimed at both terrestrial and orbital deployments, according to the analysts.

Arguably the most distinctive feature of Kessel is its 84-layer PCB midplane, which uses ultra-low-loss M10 copper-clad laminates (CCLs). By contrast, Nvidia's Kyber architecture relied on a backplane based on a considerably more complex 156-layer PCB featuring M9 CCLs. The reduction in layer count by nearly half could substantially improve manufacturability and production yields, but the more advanced copper-clad laminate will almost certainly increase material costs. In any case, an 84-layer PCB is a device that is exceptionally hard to build.

The move to a PCB midplane could simplify system assembly by eliminating numerous high-speed cable connections, but it would not necessarily reduce manufacturing costs. An 84-layer PCB that relies on ultra-low-loss M10 laminate is an exceptionally expensive component that requires sophisticated manufacturing processes and precise quality control. To put an 84-layer PCB number into context, modern high-end server motherboards use 15 – 20 layers, whereas server development boards use more than 20 layers to virtually eliminate any electrical issues with the board itself. Furthermore, manufacturing yields of an 84-layer PCB could become a major obstacle, as defects in internal layers may render an entire board unusable. Consequently, the economic viability of Kessel will depend on whether savings from cable elimination and independent component procurement can offset the cost of its complex midplane.

Perhaps more importantly, Kessel represents a departure from Nvidia's conventional system-level procurement model. Instead of purchasing Nvidia's assembled L6 compute boards or even L10 trays that Nvidia plans to sell with its Vera Rubin generation, SpaceX reportedly plans to acquire AI accelerators, CPUs, switches, and networking components directly from Nvidia and procure other components from third-party suppliers (one can wonder how easy it will be for SpaceX/xAI to procure memory amid today's shortages). This would enable SpaceX to select its own PCB manufacturers, component vendors, and manufacturing partners, optimize its hardware for its infrastructure (which will be important for orbital deployments), and perhaps reduce intermediary costs. Meanwhile, the company would assume greater responsibility for system design, validation, manufacturing quality, and supply-chain management, which is something that most hyperscalers have been doing in recent years.

For Nvidia, the implications are less straightforward. Although direct sales of CPU and AI GPU packages could reduce the company's revenue from complete compute-board assemblies, the arrangement could also encourage other large customers to develop their own Nvidia-based systems and eventually deploy more Nvidia-based machines, something that may be important in a world where custom silicon developed by hyperscalers is rapidly gaining traction. However, to make this happen, Kessel must be a smashing success that will offer clear advantages over systems designed by Nvidia.

articles.title: CoreWeave tests AI integrations on its cloud before you migrate
articles.description: Moving an AI workload to another cloud means bringing more than a model and its data. Your serving layer, observability The post CoreWeave tests AI integrations on its cloud before you migrate appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Moving an AI workload to another cloud means bringing more than a model and its data. Your serving layer, observability dashboards, security controls, and storage systems have to work together on the new infrastructure. For platform teams, proving those connections under real traffic can become the slowest and riskiest part of the move.

As a stack grows across vendors and clouds, each project adds more integration questions. A compatible specification is a starting point. It doesn’t guarantee a tool will behave as expected in production, or that the runbooks and security workflows built around it will carry over.

Make production validation visible

An integration needs to work on the infrastructure where you plan to run it, under production traffic. The tools should also be ones your team already uses or has asked for.

“A compatible specification is a starting point. It doesn’t guarantee a tool will behave as expected in production, or that the runbooks and security workflows built around it will carry over.”

We built the CoreWeave Partner Network to make that validation visible. It brings relationships with CrowdStrike, VAST Data, Reflection, IBM, and other technology vendors into a curated network of integrations tested under real-world production conditions on CoreWeave Cloud.

The network covers four parts of the AI stack, from training and inference to data movement, security, and the next iteration:

Infrastructure: compute, storage, networking, servers, and interconnects, with partners including VAST Data, Dell, AMD, IBM, BackBlaze, and Pulumi.

Data services: storing, processing, moving, and accessing AI data throughout its lifecycle, with ClickHouse, Encord, LanceDB, and Datology.

Independent software vendors (ISVs): orchestration, observability, and model development, including Grafana, Datadog, Union, SkyPilot, IBM, Pinecone, Redis, LlamaIndex, and Clockwork. A dedicated security segment includes CrowdStrike, Zscaler, and Cranium.

Models, agents, and inference: foundational software and services for building, training, serving, and scaling applications, with Reflection, RadixArk, Inferact, OpenRouter, and Red Hat.

Together, these integrations support running and observing models, curating data, improving behavior, and evaluating the next release. Every partner must meet the same requirement: an integration that works on CoreWeave infrastructure under production conditions. Partners enter the network because customers run them or ask for them.

Read the workload evidence

IBM trained its Granite models on CoreWeave around one of the first deployments of Nvidia GB200 NVL72 clusters. Cohere built North, its agentic AI platform, on one of the industry’s first production GB200 NVL72 clusters and reported training three times faster than on Nvidia Hopper.

Mistral AI trains its models entirely on CoreWeave and cites training 2.5 times faster on Nvidia GB200 NVL72 systems. Decart uses Nvidia HGX B200 at production scale through its CoreWeave collaboration, on a platform that includes Weights & Biases.

The underlying relationships predate the network announcement. CoreWeave and Weights & Biases have run production integrations with Encord, Pinecone, and other partners since the early wave of open-source large language models (LLMs) and frontier-model training.

Jon Jones, CoreWeave’s Chief Revenue Officer, describes the change as making existing partner work visible before customers build. The network also provides a repeatable way to pursue deeper integrations, joint go-to-market work, and shared innovation.

The partners emphasize different parts of that system. VAST Data co-founder and chief technology officer Alon Horev describes combining CoreWeave’s AI cloud with the VAST AI Operating System across large-scale training, fine-tuning, production inference, and continuous agentic workloads. CrowdStrike CEO and founder George Kurtz emphasizes security built into the infrastructure running AI. Adam Lawrence, general manager of IBM Americas, points to IBM and Red Hat technologies as a way to expand choice and reduce integration work when deploying and scaling AI.

Carry over the operations you already use

Your team has already built runbooks around its observability tools. Grafana and Datadog integrations let you carry that work over. CrowdStrike, Zscaler, and Cranium provide security integrations, bringing existing threat visibility and response tooling.

Inference integrations serve a similar purpose: keeping the models available as teams expand onto CoreWeave, without rebuilding the serving layer. The goal is to add capacity while retaining the parts of the stack that already work.

“A marketplace listing still leaves your team to validate the integration. An LLM can suggest what’s popular without telling you what works on your infrastructure.”

A marketplace listing still leaves your team to validate the integration. An LLM can suggest what’s popular without telling you what works on your infrastructure. We select partners based on customer demand and test their integrations across all four segments.

Include the tools your agents call

The integration problem also reaches inside agent execution. Most closed models include web search, while most open-weight models do not. Teams choosing open weights for cost, control, or customization have often had to connect a search provider separately.

CoreWeave is extending its partner approach to these tools, beginning with Exa, Parallel Web Systems, and You.com. The announced search layer provides access through one integration instead of a separate contract for each provider.

Teams can enable it through a single setting on a standard inference request or access it from inside a CoreWeave Sandbox, without setting up a separate software development kit (SDK) or account. The arrangement is nonexclusive, so using the integration does not restrict future provider choices.

We announced the search partnerships at Fully Connected, with the remaining integration work planned for the following weeks. As those integrations become available, they will meet the same production-validation standard as the rest of the network.

Start with the connections your workload needs

Before adding another cloud, check the serving, data, observability, and security connections your workload depends on. Ask which integrations have been tested under production conditions and what your team will still need to validate.

“Before adding another cloud, check the serving, data, observability, and security connections your workload depends on.”

The CoreWeave Partner Network lists validated partners. CoreWeave account teams can discuss a specific integration and workload, and partner sessions from Fully Connected 2026 offer another way to see the integrations in use. Teams interested in new collaborations can explore the partner program.

articles.title: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install
articles.description: KB5132061 throws 0x800F0993 and 0x800F0989 errors, and Redmond is saying nothing
articles.content:
Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch.

Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products. However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error.

Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch.

In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager.

In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully.

However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually.

It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal.

Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services.

The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling, with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update.

At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time.

The Register has asked Microsoft to comment. ®

articles.title: Softbank loses $3.7 billion on canceled AI data center gas turbine orders days after denying Elon Musk’s claim it was defaulting
articles.description: SoftBank might not have defaulted on a raft of gas turbine orders, but it has pulled out of deals for unwanted power units after overestimating how many it could use amid the AI data center buildout boom.
articles.content:
By early 2026, Japanese tech investment outfit SoftBank had reserved more power generation capacity than the entire state of Connecticut after cornering a huge portion of the global gas turbine production capacity. Now, the same company has chosen to take a $3.7 billion hit to its earnings after canceling reservations for the highly sought-after power generation hardware. The WSJ reports that SoftBank had reserved more than 13 gigawatts of power-producing turbines, citing unnamed "people familiar with the orders." That's the equivalent of more than six Hoover Dams' worth of capacity, with SoftBank founder and chief executive Masayoshi Son believing that it would be vital to the company's earning potential moving forward.

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

The gas turbines were to power AI data centers, and SoftBank is set to build a 9.2-gigawatt power plant in Ohio, with construction scheduled for early 2027. It'll cost $33 billion to build and will provide power to a neighboring eight-gigawatt data center. That data center will be leased to OpenAI, albeit only after Nvidia entered discussions about guaranteeing around $250 billion of financing for the project.

But SoftBank got ahead of itself. After initially planning to use the turbines for future gas-powered plants, the company has now chosen to change direction. Orders for turbines, engines that convert natural gas into the electricity used by data centers, must be placed years in advance of them being required. The company had bet big, placing huge orders with the expectation that demand would greatly outstrip supply. That would leave SoftBank in an enviable position, holding huge orders for the vital components required as part of a data center rollout boosted by AI demand. But those reservations weren't cheap — turbine manufacturers regularly charge customers tens of millions of dollars per gigawatt.

It's now canceled its remaining reservations with GE Vernova, its turbine supplier, while also unwinding contracts for orders that were too far gone. SoftBank told investors on a recent earnings call that the orders had been placed “to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortages,” but it now appears it anticipated a little too much.

Crucially, SoftBank is also keen for everyone to know that this move was voluntary and that it did not default on its orders. That's contrary to what xAI CEO Elon Musk claimed in a post on his X social network. SoftBank Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto was quick to counter Musk's claims. “This is simply not correct at all,” Goto reportedly said. “There is no such default.”

US big-hitting VCs Lightspeed and Alphabet's CapitalG have backed UK chip startup  Fractile in a £500m-plus funding round, which values the startup at over £5bn, the UK government said today in a press release.

The UK Nvidia challenger, based in Bristol and London, designs chips for AI inference, the process of running an AI model.

Founded in 2022 by Oxford PhD Walter Goodwin, Fractile’s architecture keeps data directly on the chip, unlike standard chips that must constantly shuttle data between the processor and separate memory modules.
It says this method can run LLMs up to a hundred times faster than existing hardware while lowering operational costs by 90 per cent. Fractile's specialised chips are set to be ready for data centre deployment next year.

The investment comes as the UK looks to become a leader in parts of the AI stack and build up its sovereign capabilities in critical technologies, reducing dependence on fragile overseas supply chains.

AI minister Kanishka Narayan said: “For too long, Britain has produced some of the world’s best scientific ideas, only to see too much of the technology, industry and wealth they create built elsewhere.

articles.title: NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away
articles.description: Flash VGR in Morse code on November 17 to salute the veteran probe – just don't expect it to see you
articles.content:
Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth next week, and NASA wants us to mark the occasion by flashing our lights at the sky.

The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set.

"Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18.

For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website.

According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present.

Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured.

NASA has invited the public to join in a spacecraft photo opportunity before. On July 19, 2013, Cassini photographed Earth and the Moon from its orbit around Saturn for "The Day the Earth Smiled," while people back home were encouraged to look up and "just smile at the sheer joy of being alive on a Pale Blue Dot."

Voyager 2, the spacecraft's sibling, is not expected to reach the same milestone for another nine years. It took a different path through the solar system to swing past Uranus and Neptune.

It will, however, be uncertain as to whether Voyager 2 will still be able to communicate by then – even with recent efforts to eke out the probe's dwindling power supply, margins are razor thin. ®

articles.title: Montech King 95 3D Pro case review: The King has returned
articles.description: The new Montech King 95 3D case offers 3-panel panoramic views of the inside, loads of interior space for components and cooling, and the Pro version comes with seven RGB fan
articles.content:
PC case, cooling, and PSU maker Montech is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year and has released a new flagship ATX chassis, the King 95 3D and 3D Pro. Like the previous King 95, the 3D version keeps the signature 15-degree curved-glass panoramic front panel and adds a top glass panel, giving you a third window and a unique aesthetic for viewing your build. An integrated, contoured ARGB strip follows the chassis's smooth lines, making it look every bit the king of the castle.

Inside, the large mid-tower chassis supports multiple radiators (though only one 360mm), large graphics cards (plus integrated adjustable GPU support), CPU air coolers, and spots for 2.5- and 3.5-inch drives. However, it doesn't support E-ATX motherboards. The King 95 3D supports rear-connect motherboards and has ample room for cable routing and management. The front aluminum panel IO runs vertically, as with previous King cases, and includes a fast USB 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C port. Overall, it has everything you want in a premium chassis. The uncommon three-panel view into your PC is a great way to show off your rig.

The King 95 3D is available for an inexpensive (at least for curved glass) $119.90 if you want to select your own fans. The 3D Pro includes seven pre-installed LINK Fan INF 120 fans for builders who want a more coordinated look out of the box, plus it includes the Lumi hub (a dedicated fan controller), for $199.90. We have the 3D Pro version in our lab and ran the case through thermal and noise testing in its out-of-the-box configuration to show how it performs compared to others. Will it make our best PC cases list? It has a chance. But before we get into the details, here are the case's specifications from Montech.

Features of the King 95 3D

▶️ External Features

From the outside, the King 95 3D Pro looks the part of its royal name. That signature curve and three panes of glass offer a panoramic view inside your case like few others, letting you show off your PC from even more angles. It also features a frosted, continuous LED strip running along the tiered top, right side, and bottom, adding some tasteful bling to the chassis. If you get the Pro version with the seven fans, it’s an RGB light show inside which could be polarizing. I do wish there were an option for preinstalled non-RGB fans, since the seven included ones and the infinity mirror styling may not be for everyone. Still, the curved front corner and clean lines really cement the King 95 3D as one of the better-looking panoramic cases on the market.

Future Future Future Future Future Future Up front, the removable curved glass corner with a smoked tint sets it apart from most others. On the right, the front IO panel runs vertically, with the power button on top and the LED on/off button below. It has three USB ports: one 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C and two USB 3.2 Gen1 (5 Gbps) Type-A ports. Finally, it has a 3.5mm audio jack. That continuous 118-LED strip is visible from the front, running along the top, down the right edge, and along the bottom edge. I’m not a fan of a lot of RGB, but this implementation is tasteful. You can control this lighting through the motherboard software or Montech's Lumi software, which lets you fully customize the fans and RGB strip.

The main window panel also uses a smoke-colored tint, with Montech branding in the upper-right corner, and it's secured to the frame by two captive thumbscrews on the back. To remove it, loosen the thumbscrews, slide the panel back, pull from the top, then lift it out of the slots. Easy. I have to say, the biggest problem with all this glass is keeping it pristine and fingerprint-free.

The other (metal) side panel, behind the motherboard, slots into the frame and is secured the same way. It has filtered venting along the top and side for the fans/radiator locations, plus another area for airflow near the power supply and drive mounting locations. In the middle is a gold placard with Montech King 95 3D 10th anniversary badging. Note: The dust filters on this panel aren't removable, so you’ll need to remove the whole panel to clean things up.

Future Future Future At the top, we get a better look at the third windowed panel, letting observers peer into the case from a different angle rather than straight on or from the front. We can also see the tiered top and part of the long RGB strip. Taking this panel off isn’t as simple as the rest. Yes, it’s also secured by two captive thumbscrews on the back, but to remove it, you’ll need to open the main window panel to expose a retaining screw, remove it, then loosen the back thumbscrews and slide it to the rear. After you remove the top glass, you can remove the upper and side retaining screws to take it out. When building, I didn’t find this necessary, but it’s good to know you can take it apart if needed.

Looking at the case from behind, one of the first things I noticed was the vertical PSU mounting location on the left. This space supports up to 220mm power supplies, which is all but the largest on the market. On the right, we see space for two 120mm fans, the motherboard I/O, and seven horizontal expansion slots. Unfortunately, Montech says the King 95 3D does not support vertical GPUs.

Underneath the case, there isn’t a lot going on. We get a better look at the four short rubber-bottom ‘feet’ and the removable dust filter. Montech put on its thinking cap and designed the dust filter to slide out from the front, so chances are you won’t have to move your heavy case to clean it.

▶️ Internal Features

Inside, the case uses a dual-chamber design, with the power supply and all wires hidden behind the motherboard tray. At the bottom, we see three Link Fan INF 120s (reverse blade) along with the mirror finish. The magnetically linked, daisy-chainable fans run up to 2,300 RPM (2,200 RPM on the reverse blade), pushing between 65-67 CFM with a maximum rating of 32dBA (29 dBA on the standard blade). A single Link Fan INF 120 costs $19.90, while a 3-pack (with Lumi Hub) is $64.90. If you do the math for seven fans and the Lumi Hub, it’s cheaper to buy them with the case rather than separately.

When powered on, the mirrored sides become an infinity panel, and with all seven matching, it creates a consistent view across the build. The bottom fan bracket is adjustable, with three positions (8 degrees). We left it down during testing, but with it up, you can focus more air towards the GPU and show off whatever fans you put in the space.

The motherboard tray has plenty of cutouts to access the back of the motherboard for easy installation/removal of air coolers or AIO/custom water-cooling blocks. The case also supports rear-connect ecosystems, including Asus BTF, Gigabyte Stealth, and MSI Project Zero boards. Grommets surround the motherboard tray and are in ideal locations, but like most, they pull out easily when you try to route cables, especially those with larger connectors. I wish all case vendors would secure these better, since they're a pain to reinstall, especially when the case is full of cables.

Up top, we can see the huge gap above the motherboard tray for more fans and radiators. The case cooled just fine with the seven included fans and our air cooler, though GPU temps ran a bit warmer in our noise-normalized testing. That top gap is begging to be filled with fans, even if only for aesthetics. If you plan to use an AIO cooler, this isn’t a problem, since the radiator/fans will fill the space.

Future Future Future Future Future From the front, you can see the two Link INF 120mm fans and, at the bottom, the tool-less, adjustable GPU support strut. The back has space to mount two 120mm fans or one 120mm radiator. You can also see the seven horizontal expansion slots held in by thumbnail screws.

Inside, the top of the case above the motherboard space fits up to three 120mm fans or a 360mm radiator. The space is offset back from the motherboard tray, which is a boon for cable management. Normally, there’s barely any room to route the EPS cables, but here there's plenty. Just note that if your build uses air cooling, you will need to fill that area with fans to make it look good. Otherwise, it’s just a blank open space above the motherboard.

Future Future Future On the rear side of the chassis, we get a good look at the space behind the motherboard tray and the fan baffles. There’s plenty of room to route cables, and Montech has multiple pre-installed Velcro straps for cable routing. Even with the power supply installed, there’s plenty of room underneath it to stash excess cables.

At the bottom, we see a simple ARGB hub that consolidates the three different ARGB cables from the fans into one header to control all of them. Montech also includes a magnetic Lumi fan/RGB hub (which supports up to 13 Link Fans total) with both the Pro and non-Pro variants. Oddly, it comes loose/uninstalled on the Pro, but installed on the non-Pro. The box in the lower-right holds one 3.5-inch HDD and a single 2.5-inch drive. The second 2.5-inch drive mounts in the other location at the bottom left, next to the side fans.

We do like the look of the King 95 3D Pro case in black, and I bet it looks great in white with an all-white build too. The curved glass and 3-panel panoramic interior views are great for anyone who’d like to show off their now-ridiculously expensive parts. The included Link Fan INF 120 fans work well and run relatively quietly. If there’s an aesthetic drawback, it's that I’m not a huge fan of all the RGB and infinity mirrors on the pre-installed fans. It’s a lot, and it makes me yearn for an option with preinstalled fans and no RGB. Of course, you can turn them off in the software, or buy the non-Pro and choose whichever fans fit your build.

articles.title: Inside Biscay's startup ecosystem: Industrial strengths, public investment, and deeptech ambition
articles.description: Biscay (Bizkaia), in Spain’s Basque Country, is building on its industrial heritage to develop a startup ecosystem spanning biotechnology, advanced manufacturing, energy and emerging technologies. Wit...
articles.content:
Biscay (Bizkaia), in Spain’s Basque Country, is building on its industrial heritage to develop a startup ecosystem spanning biotechnology, advanced manufacturing, energy and emerging technologies.

With public investment, R&D incentives and collaboration between businesses, research institutions and government agencies, the region is positioning itself as a destination for deeptech innovation.

I recently attended BIOSPAIN 2026 in Bilbao, where I explored the region's approach to supporting startups, its advantages, and the challenges that remain.

Building on industrial and life sciences expertise

Biscay is home to more than 300 companies, 20 research centres, four universities and leading hospitals, forming an ecosystem that generates more than €9.4 billion and supports 62,000 jobs.

The region is a major hub for the Basque Country's life sciences sector, accounting for 45 per cent of its companies and 56 per cent of revenues. Its more than 135 life sciences companies support over 27,000 jobs and generate €5.2 billion in revenue, with particular strengths in biomanufacturing and advanced therapies.

Investment continues across biotechnology, aerospace, advanced manufacturing, renewable energy and robotics.

A major bioscience and healthcare project led by I+Med will involve €72 million in investment over three years, including €28 million for R&D, and is expected to create more than 600 jobs.

The region also offers a competitive tax regime and financial incentives. Investors in innovative companies can benefit from a 35 per cent personal income tax deduction. In comparison, capital gains on exit are eligible for a 50 per cent exemption, rising to 100 per cent if reinvested in startups or technology ventures.

Professionals relocating from abroad can receive a tax exemption on up to 50 per cent of their salary for 11 years.

Companies can also access tax deductions of up to 70 per cent for R&D activities and 15–20 per cent for technological innovation.

Alongside financial incentives, Biscay has invested in specialist infrastructure, including the Energy Intelligence Centre, Basque Hydrogen Corridor, Automotive Intelligence Centre and Bizkaia Quantum Advanced Industries initiative.

An intentional approach to supporting startups

During my time in Biscay, I spoke with Olatz Goitia Urkiaga, Director General of the economic development agency BEAZ, Oscar Ugarte, Director of Seed Capital Bizkaia and Amaia Jugo, Managing Director of Bizkaia Talent.

For Goitia, one of Biscay's distinguishing features is the collaboration between public organisations, each contributing different expertise and resources.

Alongside BEAZ and Seed Capital Bizkaia, these include the provincial tax authorities and Lantik, the Provincial Council's technology company. Lantik supports access to advanced technological infrastructure, including quantum technologies, while the tax authorities can introduce measures to attract businesses and investors. Seed Capital Bizkaia provides financing and investor networks, while BEAZ offers business development and innovation support.

"What makes the system work is bringing these organisations together around the needs of companies," Goitia explains.

"These departments don't necessarily work together in the same way elsewhere. Here, we've developed relationships that allow us to coordinate their activities and provide more comprehensive support."

For a relatively small region, she believes this collaborative approach can make a significant difference in helping startups establish themselves and grow.

The support is structured around different stages of company development.

Entrepreneurs can access grants of up to €60,000 to validate ideas through prototyping, market testing and commercial analysis.

Once a business is ready to launch, the Creation of Innovative Companies programme provides grants of up to €85,000 towards incorporation, intellectual property, premises and specialist recruitment.

For companies ready to scale, Seed Capital Bizkaia, the provincial government's venture-capital company, provides financing through participating loans and equity investment.

Public and private capital: A different approach to startup funding

Founded in 1989,

was established when few organisations were willing to take the risks of investing in early-stage companies. According to its Director Ugarte, its approach combines public and private capital, with banks participating both as shareholders and co-investors in its funds.

"What makes us distinctive is that we combine public and private capital. Banks are among our shareholders, and they also participate as co-investors in our funds," he explains.

The organisation manages investment instruments spanning seed funding, growth capital and social impact, alongside a crowdfunding platform.

"Our role is to take risks that other investors might not be prepared to take, while bringing private capital into the ecosystem."

Seed Capital Bizkaia typically provides around 40 to 50 per cent of a funding round, with private investors covering the remainder. Ugarte says the organisation is also willing to experiment with financing models that might seem unusual for a public institution.

"When we speak to other public administrations in Europe, we sometimes realise that we're doing things quite differently.

Sometimes we take approaches that might seem unusual for a public institution. But the objective is to respond quickly and provide practical support."

Crowdfunding brings local investors into the ecosystem.

One example is Seed Capital Bizkaia's crowdfunding platform, established in 2019 to let ordinary citizens help finance local projects. The platform focuses on innovative businesses and projects delivering positive environmental or social impact. Its current approach centres on lending, with financing rounds typically ranging from €100,000 to €200,000. Ugarte says demand has been encouraging:

"We recently completed a round in just eight minutes. People are waiting for opportunities to invest because they're interested in the projects and the returns."

Beyond raising capital, the platform introduces residents to innovative companies operating nearby that they might otherwise never encounter. "We see it as a combination of financial participation, community engagement and promoting local talent," he says.

From industrial innovation to GovTech

Biscay's industrial base also provides opportunities for startups developing technologies for established sectors, particularly energy, automotive and healthcare. Ugarte says the region's research institutions, hospitals and industrial expertise have helped establish a strong foundation for innovation.

"We started supporting health and biotech projects around 30 years ago. We have universities, doctors, researchers and healthcare institutions that provide a strong foundation for innovation."

Seed Capital Bizkaia typically backs one to three new healthcare projects annually, although biotechnology requires a longer investment horizon.

Beyond industry, Biscay is encouraging startups to develop solutions for public administration through a GovTech initiative that has been running for around three years. One of the biggest challenges, Goitia says, has been changing how government departments approach procurement and innovation.

"Public administrations are accustomed to buying existing products and services. But sometimes those solutions don't meet their needs."

The initiative encourages departments to identify problems and explore whether startups could develop more effective solutions. This has involved training public-sector teams, including procurement staff, to work differently with innovative companies.

"We now identify around three to five public-sector challenges each year. The idea is to give innovative companies opportunities to develop solutions to real problems within public administration."

From startup to scaleup: Closing the funding gap

Despite its support for early-stage companies, helping startups scale remains a challenge, particularly for those moving into industrial production, much like elsewhere in Europe.

Goitia acknowledges:

"The challenge comes when they need to scale, particularly when that involves industrial production. That's an area where we still need to strengthen the ecosystem."

Ugarte, however, argues that Biscay's comparatively affordable talent and research infrastructure give companies a reason to maintain their operations in the region:

"If you compare the cost of operating here with somewhere like Boston, the difference can be significant. Boston has access to enormous amounts of investment capital, but companies also face much higher costs for talent and infrastructure."

Seed Capital Bizkaia is also building international investor relationships through its fund-of-funds activities, including investments in funds in Estonia and Portugal.

The aim is to connect local companies with specialist investors and create relationships that can bring additional capital and expertise into the region.

"We've spent years developing these relationships, and that makes a real difference. It's not simply about having funding available. It's about helping companies access the knowledge, partnerships and infrastructure they need."

Attracting international talent — and giving people reasons to stay

Access to skilled workers is another priority. Bizkaia Talent is a nonprofit initiative backed by the Provincial Council of Bizkaia and leading Basque companies and universities, working to attract, develop and retain highly skilled professionals.

According to its managing director, Amaia Jugo, the organisation works closely with employers to understand their recruitment needs and supports international professionals considering relocation.

"We work with a wide range of businesses, particularly SMEs, which have very different needs. We also help professionals who are considering moving to Bizkaia for work.

However, support goes beyond finding employment to support with practical matters such as housing, schools and other services people need when relocating.

"The goal isn’t simply to attract professionals to the region, but to help them settle here and encourage them to stay."

The region's industrial economy creates particular demand for specialised technical skills, including industrial automation.

Bizkaia Talent is developing initiatives to connect employers with qualified professionals from countries such as Colombia and Peru, where skilled workers may have fewer local employment opportunities. It also supports pathways from education into industry, including placements that allow international students to gain work experience with local companies.

Jugo emphasises the importance of designing these initiatives around employers' actual needs.

"Sometimes public institutions develop programmes without listening closely enough to the people they're supposed to support. We try to do the opposite."

Companies that have established operations in Biscay include Woza Labs, a climate tech startup that relocated from London to Bilbao and uses AI-driven climate modelling to help companies such as Iberdrola strengthen electricity grids against extreme weather.

Another is Satlantis, an Earth observation company founded in Florida that subsequently established its headquarters in Biscay while retaining US operations. Its technology provides high-resolution satellite imaging for applications including methane emissions detection. ​

Founded in 2022 as a spin-off from Spanish biotech company Algenex, Cocoon Bioscience uses insects in their chrysalis stage as natural bioreactors to manufacture proteins.

Its CrisBio platform produces recombinant proteins, including enzymes and growth factors used in pharmaceuticals, life sciences and cultivated meat.

Creator advertising
platform Tano has raised $4 million in a seed funding round led by Cherry Ventures, bringing its total funding to $5 million following earlier backing
from Seedcamp and The Players Fund.

Founded by Will Caplan and
Sagar Shah, Tano develops an AI-powered platform designed to help brands manage
creator partnerships and turn influencer marketing into a more scalable and
measurable advertising channel.

As consumer attention
increasingly shifts towards content creators, brands are investing more in
influencer marketing to reach audiences and drive sales. However, managing
large numbers of creator partnerships remains complex and resource-intensive,
requiring brands to identify suitable creators, coordinate campaigns, manage
payments and measure performance. Traditional agency models can make smaller
partnerships particularly expensive, limiting opportunities to work with a
broader network of creators.

Tano aims to address these
challenges by combining AI agents with creator strategists to streamline
different stages of creator advertising. Its platform handles creator
recruitment, product seeding, communication, rewards and payments, allowing
brands to run ongoing campaigns across thousands of relationships rather than
relying on individual partnerships.

The system also uses
campaign performance data to improve creator selection and engagement over
time. Through tracking links, discount codes and commerce integrations, brands
can measure the impact of creator activity on sales, while selected content can
be repurposed for paid advertising with the necessary permissions.

Will Caplan, co-founder
and CEO of Tano, said:

Brands should be able to
set a commercial objective and invest predictably into creator advertising,
just like they invest in Meta or Google. 

Our vision is to build the
world’s largest advertising channel for commerce, powered by people. We want to
harness millions of creative minds without losing the individual perspectives
that make their content valuable. That is The Creator Advertising Platform
we’re building.

The new funding will be
used to hire additional engineers and creator strategists, supporting further
development and improvement of Tano's platform as the company works to scale
its creator advertising operations.

articles.title: Colin Farrell Says 'There's a Conversation to Be Had' About The Penguin Season 2, Having Filmed Just 2 Scenes for The Batman Part II
articles.description: Colin Farrell has confirmed he only appears in two scenes as the Penguin in The Batman Part II, but would love to play the character again in a potential Season 2 of the HBO show, insisting "there's a conversation to be had."
articles.content:
Colin Farrell has confirmed he only appears in two scenes as the Penguin in The Batman Part II, but would love to play the character again in a potential Season 2 of the HBO show, insisting "there's a conversation to be had."

Farrell is set to don the prosthetics once again as the Penguin in The Batman Part II, now due out February 18, 2028, having played the character first in The Batman and again in the well-received The Penguin HBO Max show.

In an interview on UK show This Morning to promote his upcoming film The Slightest Touch, Farrell was asked about playing the Penguin once again.

“I'd love to. I'd love to do a second season. There's a conversation to be had,” he replied. Farrell then talked about his role in The Batman Part II.

“So the Batman film, they're doing the sequel to The Batman, and I did two scenes in that. Just that. In and out. It was a bit tasty to do it. I was kind of moaning about the makeup again, but I do love the character and I'm very protective of the character. And there's definitely a conversation to be had about doing a second season.”

The Batman movies are from writer and director Matt Reeves, who recently drafted in Ocean's 11 director Steven Soderbergh to help him finish principal photography on the sequel while he deals with a personal matter. Those Batman films, alongside The Penguin TV show, form part of what is called The Batman Epic Crime Saga, which is separate to James Gunn’s rebooted DC Universe.

Gunn’s plan was to introduce a Batman of his own with The Brave and the Bold, but after this week’s dramatic news about his and fellow DC Studios co-CEO Peter Safran's exit from the company, the future of the DCU and indeed a third potential Batman movie from Matt Reeves is up in the air. New Warner Bros. owner Skydance has yet to outline its plans for DC movies and TV shows, with both Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow and Reeves’ The Batman Part II still down for release in theaters.

As for Farrell, in June he said he had read The Batman Part II script, which was written by Reeves and Mattson Tomlin, and loved it. Speaking to ScreenRant, Farrell described the script, and his involvement in the movie.

"I got to read from the first to last page and it's really magnificent,” he said. “I just think Matt Reeves is brilliant and he wrote, not only tonally, a really kind of dark and at times terrifying piece, and not only psychologically weighty and nuanced, but really feeling. It's a really... There's moments in it. It's full of feeling. I just think he wrote kind of a contemporary genre masterpiece, really. I'm only in two scenes, which is great because it means I can enjoy the rest of the film."

articles.title: Nintendo unleashes DMCA takedown wave against open-source Switch modchip firmware, 144 tools disabled
articles.description: Nintendo is going after the open-source firmware behind hardware modchips on Nintendo Switch
articles.content:
Nintendo has set its famously litigious sights on the open-source firmware that powers hardware modchips on Nintendo Switch. Earlier this week, GitHub posted a DCMA request from Nintendo of America confirming that an entire network of 144 total repositories, including the parent repository, was taken down. Mod chip firmware for hardware including SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, and HWFLY was targeted.

Early original Nintendo Switch consoles shipped with an unpatchable hardware exploit found in the device's recovery mode, which has since been patched in later units such as the Switch Lite and Switch OLED (the modchip hack doesn't work on Switch 2). As such, running custom software on patched Switches requires hardware modification, soldering a microchip like a Picofly, HWFLY, or SX Core to your Switch's motherboard. These chips require firmware, specifically code that can perform the voltage glitching required during boot to hack the Switch.

Rather than playing whack-a-mole with vendors of off-the-shelf microcontrollers, Nintendo has instead issued a DCMA takedown notice to the entire family of GitHub repos hosting this firmware. "The reported repositories offer, link to, or otherwise provide access to mod chip firmware including but not limited to SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, or HWFLY," the DCMA request from Nintendo reads. "The firmware allows Nintendo Switch modchips to illegally circumvent Nintendo’s TPMs in order to run illegal copies of Nintendo Switch games. Specifically, during operation, the mod chip firmware at the reported repositories circumvents the technological protection measures put in place on the Nintendo Switch console by bypassing the boot sequence.

Nintendo went on to state that because these repositories are designed "primarily" to unlawfully circumvent technological measures controlling access to work protected under the DCMA, distributing mod chip firmware "constitutes unlawful trafficking in technology that is 'primarily designed or produced for the purpose of circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access' to copyrighted works." In support of this argument, Nintendo cited criminal proceedings brought by the US Department of Justice against Team-Xecuter, a maker and seller of SX Pro, SX Core, and SX Lite modchips.

While these modchips can be (and are) used for game piracy, they unlock a host of features including running homebrew and custom applications, emulation, alternative operating systems, and more. They also enable game modding, custom themes, and even Switch overclocking. Naturally, Nintendo has chosen to focus on their utility in accessing pirated games and bypassing DRM.

Because much of this hardware and firmware is already out in the wild, the move won't have any impact on existing Switch owners who have a modchip installed. However, this will prevent firmware updates to existing modchips, as well as firmware flashing and reflashing. Naturally, it will also prevent future potential hardware modders from hacking their Switch in the same way.

Nintendo is famous for its fervent prosecution of copyright law, but developments in AI are turning this into a drastically more complicated battle. Nintendo's Zelda remake was dumped online on the same day it launched on Switch 2, while earlier this year one developer used AI to bring the original Nintendo 64 version to iOS. In July, Mario Kart Wii was recompiled for PC in 4K with over 200 tracks.
