articles.title: Ukrainian drone operations squeezed by fiber optic cable shortage triggered by AI data center buildouts
articles.description: Ukrainian drone manufacturer BlueBird Tech says that limited fiber optic supplies are making it harder to build jam-proof fiber optic drones.
articles.content:
Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine sparked a new era of drone warfare. Russian invaders first used drones with fiber-optic tethers to combat electronic warfare on the front lines, but both sides now use these jam-proof drones. Against that backdrop, the AI data center buildout is making it harder for Ukraine to buy the fiber-optic spools that it needs to continue scaling its drone manufacturing capabilities. A research and development representative for BlueBird Tech, a Ukrainian defense firm specializing in drones, told Ars Technica in an interview that prices of fiber optic cables have risen around six to 10 times in the past couple of years as AI data center demand soaks up more and more of the supply of this resource.

According to that interview, It’s estimated that Ukraine and Russia are producing around 50,000 fiber optic drones monthly, with each drone capable of ranges of up to 62 miles. But Ukraine has only been able to acquire 72 miles of fiber optic cable from Chinese suppliers during August 2025, whereas Russia imported a whopping 328,000 miles during that same month. It was estimated that Russia acquired 37 million miles of fiber during the entirety of 2025, accounting for over 10% of the global production.

What makes matters worse for Ukrainian defenders is that there is an estimated 111-million-mile shortfall in fiber optic cable supply across the world, adding to the various shortages that the data center industry has faced in recent years. Aside from the material shortfall, Ukraine faces trade barriers in acquiring more fiber. The BlueBird representative claimed that some Chinese companies have outright refused to sell Ukraine fiber optic cables.

China is the primary supplier of this material, so it’s easier for Russia to obtain them through its massive land border with the country. While Ukraine could purchase fiber optic cables from suppliers located in other countries, that's not much of an alternative. The BlueBird rep notes: "there can be intermediaries in other countries, and prices can differ depending on the country and the purchasing route. But in the end, China remains the main source of the fiber optic material we are talking about.”

There has also been talk of producing fiber optic cables domestically in Ukraine, but such manufacturing requires specially trained personnel who must practice on the already limited supply of fiber optic cables. Even if manufacturers automate production, they still require experienced personnel who can oversee the line and ensure the quality of the final product.

The data center build out has been causing all kinds of shortages. We’ve seen supply shortfalls in GPUs, memory chips, and even PCBs, but there’s also shortages in other seemingly unrelated industries like power infrastructure, optical transceivers, and even in critical skilled labor like electricians. This overwhelming demand has started affecting other industries not related to computing, like cars, home construction, and now, fiber optic attack drones.

articles.title: Tendrils Compute raises $30M to “redo the CPU”
articles.description: A UK startup developing a radically different type of computer chip has raised $30m in a reported hotly contested funding round.Cambridge-based Tendrils Compute is looking to challenge the dominance o...
articles.content:
A UK startup developing a radically different type of computer chip has raised $30m in a reported hotly contested funding round.

Cambridge-based Tendrils Compute is looking to challenge the dominance of conventional CPU and GPU architecture.
Tendrils is one of several UK chip companies, along with Olix and Fractile, which investors are backing.

Tendrils believes that general-purpose chips based on its computing model, called interaction nets, will scale without the cost diffilculties and historical designed problems linked with current CPUs.

Its technology allows it to run thousands of small processes at the same time and handle complex workloads.

Explaining its tech, Tendrils said: "Instead of starting from a sequential design, we’re building our processor to have thousands of cores operating in parallel. This requires moving beyond the notion of shared mutable memory and linear instruction sequences. To make this possible, we’re working in tandem on the open-source language Vine, which has been designed from the beginning to target a new wave of parallel-first architectures."

The startup has yet to disclose any hardware benchmarks, disclosing its performance levels.

The round, which was reportedly hotly contested, was led by Benchmark with participation from Visionaries Clubs, the UK Sovereign AI Fund, FR8, Antimatter, Cloudberry VC, Conviction, Embassy Ventures, and SV Angels.

articles.title: Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens
articles.description: Anything Windows can bork, the penguin can bork sideways
articles.content:
UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better.

Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem.

There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd, an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT. Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear.

Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands.

The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery.

Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap – at least until AI ate all the RAM – and low-powered compared with a full-fat Windows PC. Heathrow's senior product owner for displays described the approach as a "reliable, secure solution that has a significantly lower hardware cost and are 30-40% more energy efficient than our previous hardware."

Readers might be interested to know that Heathrow has spent years working on its new screens. The product owner again: "We've completely re-engineered our content distribution system to be flexible and device-agnostic."

So Windows in one place, and Linux somewhere else. All rubbing along famously. Assuming, of course, the displays can show more than a virtual cough and splutter during boot. ®

articles.title: AMD: Where we're going we don't need (as much) DRAM
articles.description: The House of Zen's Mext team promises smarter SWAP through the power of, you'll never guess: AI
articles.content:
AMD's latest sales pitch: Up to 99 percent of the performance with half the DRAM, provided you're willing to buy a Mext license alongside your shiny new Epyc server.

This is made possible by using AI models to load memory pages in and out of cheaper NVMe storage before your operating system or apps ever know they need it — kind of like SWAP or a Windows page file, but smarter.

AMD acquired the tech from Mext back in June, and according to former CEO Gary Smerdon — now CVP of business development at AMD — the tech could cut enterprise server costs by as much as 83 percent by replacing costly RDIMMs with flash storage. Of the initial 145 systems the software has been deployed on so far, he estimates customers have already saved $5 million in avoided DRAM costs.

"Conservatively, 60, 70, even 80 or 90 percent for very large memory systems, of the cost of a server can be in memory," he explained.

Everyone's favorite buzzword to the rescue

Even in systems with high memory utilization, where (say) 95 percent of the memory is "in use," a lot of it isn't actively being used, he explained. He cited a Meta research paper that showed that between 50 and 80 percent of memory pages hadn't been touched in five minutes, ten minutes, or even longer. "Five minutes to Epyc is an eternity."

Mext technology aims to offload those infrequently accessed pages to flash. The challenge, Smerdon explains, is that while flash may be 50x cheaper per bit, 30x lower power per bit, it's also 500x slower.

This is why most folks, when provisioning VPCs or servers, generally avoid swapping out to disk wherever possible: it kills application performance and sends service level agreements out the window.

So for Mext's tech to work, it needed to ensure that any pages offloaded to storage were back in DRAM before they're needed. Kind of like running an errand in the middle of the workday – so long as you're back before your boss needs you again, they'll never know you left your desk.

The problem was that the "R" in DRAM stands for random. Predicting which pages the system was going to need at which time isn't exactly trivial. The solution? (Brace for it.)

"We realized we could use AI to monitor the system and proactively push those pages back into DRAM, so that as far as the application or the operating system knew, they were there the whole time," Smerdon said. In other words: "We transparently make flash appear as DRAM."

So, "instead of buying two terabytes of DRAM for your Epyc-based server, you could buy one terabyte of DRAM, and then the next terabyte comes with Mext."

To do this, AMD’s Mext employs a number of machine learning algorithms.

"The workhorse model is a transformer derivative model, just like ChatGPT or Claude or the other famous models, but instead of predicting, for example, in the case of text, what word is next, what we're doing is predicting what page of memory is going to be required next," Smerdon explained. So long as the pages are in DRAM before they're needed, the pages don't even need to be in the right order, he added.

Training the models to predict memory access patterns accurately presents its own challenges, which, Smerdon says, makes pre-training the models impractical.

Instead, they take a single Epyc core and train the model "in under one second," he explained. From there, the model is further refined and retrained over time until it is able to predict accurately where the pages need to be and when they need to be there.

All of this training, he emphasizes, takes place on the CPU core — no GPU required, which means essentially any Epyc customer can take advantage of the software platform.

While no GPU may be required, it's worth noting that in virtualized environments, the software requires one core per VM or VPC, so the overhead scales with virtualization. Container runtimes presumably don't suffer from this same limitation. We've reached out to AMD for clarification.

99 percent of the perf, half the DRAM

According to AMD, the technology actually works. Initially, Smerdon says, the company targeted memory-hungry applications like electronic design automation (EDA) and content creation, but later expanded to support latency-sensitive applications like databases and agentic AI pipelines.

"When pages of memory are cold, we can push them off to flash, and there's literally no impact on performance," he said.

Smerdon is overstating things just a little here. Depending on the application and how much memory is offloaded to flash, there is a performance penalty.

According to tests against Synopsys' PrimeTime EDA suite, he claims, half the memory can be offloaded to flash using Mext and the system still achieves 95 percent of the performance of DRAM. With 25 percent DRAM and 75 percent flash, performance fell to 80 percent of the DRAM-only baseline in AMD's tests.

EDA tools are extremely memory-hungry, but the amount of data the cores are working on at any given moment is often measured in megabytes. This is why AMD's Epyc X-chips remain so popular with EDA customers and why Mext targeted it initially.

In other scenarios, like Apache Spark, AMD's Mext team says it is seeing 99 percent of the performance even after replacing half the DRAM in the system with flash.

While implementing the tech may cost some performance, AMD is betting that customers will be willing to make that compromise in exchange for substantial DRAM savings, as memory remains constrained thanks to the AI datacenter buildout.

Right now, AMD is working to integrate Mext into its broader enterprise portfolio. The software, we're told, will be exclusive to AMD hardware and will be offered as a license sold through OEM partners.

Systems running Linux require only a kernel driver to take advantage of the software, while a separate RAM View application is being offered to help enterprises understand which systems and workloads it should be enabled on.

The chip designer says it's currently in the first phase of its Mext rollout, which means working with OEMs like HPE to ensure systems are so-called "Mext ready." In the second phase, the company aims to begin selling licenses for the software and shipping Epyc platforms with RAM View preinstalled.®

articles.title: Why do some patients respond to drugs and others don't? Switchpoint Bio raises $5.3M to find out
articles.description: Emerging from stealth, Helsinki-Cambridge biotech startup Switchpoint Bio has raised $5.3 million in a pre-seed financing round, including a $5 million investment from Treehouse Delmar Investments.Mo...
articles.content:
Emerging from stealth, Helsinki-Cambridge biotech startup Switchpoint Bio has raised  $5.3 million in a pre-seed financing round, including a $5 million investment from Treehouse Delmar Investments.

Modern medicines increasingly target precise biological mechanisms, yet once treatment begins, it can be difficult to see how an individual patient’s underlying biology is actually changing and why one patient responds while another does not.

Clinical endpoints can take months or years to read out, tissue biopsies are invasive and difficult to repeat, and conventional blood biomarkers often track outcomes without explaining the biology behind them. 

The company is advancing a new way to measure those changes from blood. Circulating immune cells carry epigenomic marks of disease, exposures and treatment.

Switchpoint Bio combines precision epigenomic profiling and AI to read that record, aiming to give drug developers a scalable view of how disease and treatment change human biology. 

For drug developers, treatment response provides an immediate application: What biology is present before treatment? What changes after a drug is given, by how much, and in what way? What persists despite treatment?

Making those changes measurable over time could provide an earlier and more direct view of mechanism, response and resistance, helping drug developers understand which patients benefit, which do not, and why. 

“Drug developers need to know not only whether a patient responds, but what biology changed, what persisted and why,” said Samuel Myllykangas, PhD, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Switchpoint Bio.

“Our goal is to make these biological switchpoints visible from a routine blood sample, repeatedly and at the scale required for drug development.”

From deep cellular biology to a scalable blood measurement 

Recent advances in epigenomics, single-cell biology, population-scale datasets and AI are making it possible to connect scalable blood measurements to the underlying cellular biology of disease.  Single-cell multiomic technologies (which analyse multiple types of biological data, such as DNA, RNA and proteins, within individual cells) can provide detailed insights into how cells function.

However, they typically require fresh samples, complex processing and specialised laboratory procedures, making them difficult to use repeatedly across large numbers of patients and at multiple stages of clinical development.

Switchpoint Bio is developing a scalable approach based on targeted DNA methylation profiling directly from blood. Its assay focuses on epigenomically active regions relevant to disease and immune biology, giving deep, cost-efficient coverage of the parts of the methylome that matter most for drug development. 

Built at the intersection of genomics, epigenomics and drug development 

The company was founded by Samuel Myllykangas, PhD, and Jason Buenrostro, PhD, collaborators since developing targeted sequencing technologies together at Stanford University. Buenrostro, a MacArthur Fellow, is a professor at Harvard University, Director of the Epigenomics Program at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, and inventor of ATAC-seq, a foundational epigenomic profiling technology.

Myllykangas previously built and scaled Blueprint Genetics, which was acquired by Quest Diagnostics in 2020. 

They were joined by three co-founders: Niilo Färkkilä, PhD, Chief Commercial Officer, who brings pharmaceutical industry experience from Amgen and GSK; Jussi Paananen, PhD, Chief Technology Officer, who previously served as CTO at Blueprint Genetics; and Mitja Kurki, PhD, Scientific Advisor, who brings experience in population genomics and pharmaceutical data platforms from FinnGen, a nationwide biobank study spanning more than 500,000 participants. Paananen and Kurki have both previously worked as scientists at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. 

The company is now moving from platform development into clinical and industry validation. Switchpoint Bio is testing its approach in autoimmune disease, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), to determine whether it can epigenomically identify disease-relevant immune states from blood and follow them longitudinally through treatment. 

In parallel, Switchpoint Bio is in active discussions with pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies to define its first industry validation programs, with treatment response emerging as a key area of interest. 

“We take a long-term view, backing science we believe can genuinely change how disease is understood and treated,” said Dave Proctor of Treehouse Delmar Investments.

“Switchpoint Bio brings together exceptional scientific talent with a real path to turning breakthrough biology into evidence that helps patients, and we’re proud to support that work.”

  The financing will support continued clinical and industry validation, expansion of the company’s clinical and biobank datasets, further development of its epigenomic and AI platform, and growth of its scientific and technical team across Helsinki and Cambridge.

articles.content:
A German unicorn looking to digitise the traditional freight industry today said it had raised €228m in equity and debt, as it looks to expand its network and bolster its technology.

Sennder  is a so-called freight forwarder, connecting businesses needing to transport goods by road with available trucking companies. It has raised €73 million in equity from existing investors, led by Scanai, the Swedish transport company, and Poste Italiane, Italy's postal service.

The €155m debt facility is split into three: a €100 million credit facility with Coface, a €40 million facility with the European Investment Bank (EIB) and a €15 million facility with Deutsche Bank.

The new financing follows Berlin-based sennder raising €26 million in 2026. It is unclear what valuation its latest raise was made at. It was last publicly valued at around $2bn in 2022.

Sennder leverages AI, software and data to modernise Europe’s fragmented road freight industry. Shippers use it to find trucks to transport goods across Europe while haulers find loads for their trucks, reducing empty journeys.

Founded in 2015 and headquartered in Berlin, it says it manages more than 150,000 shipments a month.

The funding will be used to support the integration of the European road freight business it bought from US company CH Robinson, which sennder acquired in 2024.

It will also be used to expand its core transport network and the rollout of its technology platform and AI agents to shippers, carriers and other freight companies.

David Nothacker, co-founder and CEO of sennder, said: “Over the past ten years, we have built sennder through innovation and scale. With profitability achieved, we now have the financial flexibility to accelerate our next phase of growth.”

Kardi Ai develops a technology platform for
long-term heart rhythm monitoring and the early detection of potential heart
rhythm disorders. Its solution combines a fitness chest strap equipped with an
electrocardiogram (ECG) sensor, a mobile application and AI-powered analysis of
ECG recordings.

Traditional cardiac examinations typically
capture heart activity over a limited period, potentially missing
irregularities that occur intermittently. Kardi Ai aims to address this
limitation by enabling patients to monitor their heart rhythm during everyday
activities, generating data that can help physicians identify potential
problems and determine whether further medical attention is needed. The system
does not provide diagnoses but supports clinical decision-making through
long-term monitoring and analysis.

In the Czech Republic, Kardi Ai works with more
than 70 hospitals and over 20 corporate and employee-benefit partners, with its
technology used by more than 6,000 people. According to the company, its
monitoring system has identified possible cardiac arrhythmias in approximately
one quarter of users, including more than 500 findings classified as critical.

The company has also expanded into Slovakia,
where it works with more than 20 physicians, primarily cardiologists, following
its market entry several months ago.

Beyond its domestic market, Kardi Ai has
established operations in Poland, Romania and Bulgaria, while preparing to
enter Germany following the completion of pilot projects. The company has also
secured regulatory approvals supporting its planned expansion into India and
the United Arab Emirates, and is completing the medical device approval process

articles.title: UK's 'buy British' tech ambitions hit reality as less than £1 in £6 stays at home
articles.description: Whitehall's biggest IT suppliers are overwhelmingly foreign, and Uncle Sam is making a killing
articles.content:
The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech.

A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered.

A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft.

In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending.

Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers.

And the money isn't exactly being spread around. Just 150 companies receive 83 percent of public sector technology spending, with the largest 15 accounting for almost half. Smaller suppliers aren't getting much of a look-in either, receiving just 12 percent of government technology spending compared with 27 percent of spending across government as a whole.

Competition is another concern. According to IPPR, 89.9 percent of government IT contracts over the past 12 months had no published record of how many suppliers bid for the work, making it difficult to assess how competitive those procurements were.

Things get murkier when AI enters the picture, naturally. Government spending records show relatively little money going directly to the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, but that doesn't mean Whitehall isn't buying their technology. Much of it is bundled into existing cloud agreements, enterprise software licenses, and partnerships.

One example is NHS England's rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to 505,000 staff, which IPPR says was carried out under a national licensing agreement signed in June 2023, before Copilot was even generally available.

That means AI tools can reach hundreds of thousands of public sector workers through deals negotiated before those products were on the market, potentially leaving rival suppliers without an opportunity to compete.

The report, Locked In: A Realist's Agenda for Digital Sovereignty, warns that Britain's dependence on American technology could become particularly troublesome if Washington restricts access to advanced AI systems. It points to recent US restrictions on Anthropic models and limits on early access for Britain's AI Security Institute as evidence that such concerns are no longer entirely hypothetical.

The government has already committed £500 million to a Sovereign AI Fund, but researchers reckon throwing money at homegrown technology companies won't be enough to loosen Silicon Valley's grip.

Instead, they want Whitehall to negotiate technology contracts as a single customer, make it easier to switch suppliers, and work with countries including France, Germany, Japan, and South Korea to secure access to advanced AI.

Roa Powell, senior research fellow at IPPR, said: "But we cannot do it alone, and building domestic capability can't be our only bet. The UK should be working with other middle powers, pooling our buying power to shape markets and using shared leverage to secure access to frontier AI."

Darren Jones MP, who wrote the report's foreword, made a similar argument, saying Britain should work with international allies rather than attempting to build everything itself.

"We can change how the state buys technology, back industries where the UK has a genuine opportunity to lead the world, and shape markets – but we can't go it alone. We need to join with natural allies like France, Germany, Japan and Korea and make ourselves indispensable together," he said.

Whitehall might have grand plans for digital sovereignty, but it's going to be a tough sell when so much of its technology comes from across the Atlantic. And with AI already bundled into software contracts worth billions, US tech giants aren't making it easy for the government to shop elsewhere. ®

articles.title: The future of frontend starts with the design system [Sponsored]
articles.description: Over the past 20 years, the technologies used to create digital experiences have evolved dramatically. Yet the process of bringing an idea online has remained largely unchanged.Marketing and design te...
articles.content:
Over the past 20 years, the technologies used to create digital experiences have evolved dramatically. Yet the process of bringing an idea online has remained largely unchanged.

Marketing and design teams create concepts, define layouts and prepare content that development teams must translate into code before publication. Every new campaign or adaptation can introduce another technical step, affecting delivery times and limiting the autonomy of the teams responsible for the experience.

Artificial intelligence has accelerated code generation, but it has not necessarily removed this dependency. It can make an existing workflow faster without changing its underlying structure.

This raises a broader question for businesses: rather than accelerating the existing process, could the industry rethink why digital experiences still need to be translated into code in the first place?

Design System-to-Market: Rethinking the frontend workflow.

Frontend creation remains fragmented, slow and costly. Disconnected tools, teams and workflows add complexity and limit efficiency, while the frontend remains heavily dependent on hard-coded development.

Although IT teams play an essential role in ensuring performance, security, scalability and governance, not every creative change should require technical intervention. The challenge is to give business teams greater autonomy without compromising the technology behind the experience.

A different approach begins with the design system. Rather than treating it as a reference that developers must interpret and rebuild, the design system can become the foundation from which digital experiences are created, adapted and published.

This is the principle behind Design System-to-Market, the approach introduced by Live Story, the no-code platform developed to help businesses design and publish digital experiences.

The evolution of Live Story builds on the experience gained from working alongside more than 150 enterprise brands across different sectors, from finance to fashion and luxury, including Max Mara Fashion Group, Dolce & Gabbana and Guess.

The model enables marketing, creative and e-commerce teams to work directly with their brand's components, content and visual rules, without requiring a separate development process for every new experience.

AI and human creativity: Moving beyond code generation.

The growing adoption of AI makes this distinction increasingly relevant. AI agents can generate digital interfaces from natural-language prompts, but producing an initial result is only part of the creative process.

Digital experiences must also reflect brand guidelines, adapt to different markets and devices, and accommodate ongoing changes. When every adjustment requires another prompt or round of code generation, creative teams remain dependent on technical processes, adding time and costs.

Live Story approaches this differently. AI agents can generate experiences from prompts, while users can refine individual elements directly through a visual editor, modifying layouts, content and creative details without additional prompts, AI tokens or code.

This allows AI to contribute to the creative process without replacing human judgement. For businesses, it also means AI-generated experiences can remain editable, reusable and consistent with established brand standards.

Design system, components and AI within one platform.

Introduced today, 11 November, the new Live Story brings together the tools needed to turn a creative project into a published digital experience, from campaign and experiential pages to product pages.

At its centre is Live Story Studio, a no-code visual editor that enables teams to start directly from design to create pixel-perfect, responsive digital experiences, manage content independently and adapt pages across different markets, languages and digital touchpoints. Live Story Components allows teams to create reusable components aligned with their design system, providing a shared foundation for creative execution.

Through the Live Story MCP, the platform connects with design tools and AI agents, such as Figma, ChatGPT, Claude and Cursor. Teams can start from existing designs or generate new experiences through natural-language prompts, using their own components and brand rules to guide the creation process. The resulting experiences can then be refined directly in the visual editor, giving teams full control over every change without consuming additional AI tokens or writing code.

Live Story Delivery completes the workflow by publishing these experiences to existing websites, without requiring businesses to replace their technology stack.

“With the new Live Story, we have brought design, AI collaboration and publishing together into a single workflow. Our goal is to overcome the fragmentation that has long slowed down the creation of digital experiences, reducing time-to-market and giving businesses greater agility and control over their frontend,” says Stefano Mocellini, CEO and Founder of Live Story.

The evolution reflects a shift in responsibility: giving the people who understand the brand greater control over its frontend, while IT teams continue to manage the underlying technology. More about this approach and the new platform can be found on the Live Story launch page.

Growth engines: Towards a new generation of digital experiences.

The launch also marks the beginning of a new development phase for Live Story. Among the areas of innovation are growth engines, already being tested in pilot projects with customer brands, opening up new possibilities for interaction, conversation and personalisation.

The vision extends beyond individual web pages towards an ecosystem where design systems, data, content and components provide the foundation for dynamic, brand-consistent digital experiences tailored to each user, with the aim of driving measurable business results through higher conversion rates and revenue growth.

The broader implication is a change in how businesses approach the frontend: not simply as the final technical output of a design process, but as an environment that can be continuously shaped by the teams responsible for the customer experience.

Rather than focusing exclusively on faster code generation, the next phase of frontend innovation may depend on eliminating the need to write code for every new digital experience.

Live Story will explore this approach in a dedicated webinar on 18 November, titled “From brief to live: create digital experiences without the dev queue with Live Story”, examining how design systems, reusable components and AI can support the journey from campaign brief to publication.

articles.title: OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models
articles.description: How much damage can a rogue agent do in 35 seconds? Asking cos that’s how long it might take to shut one down
articles.content:
In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior.

“As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post.

The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.”

The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster.

“The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises.

A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.”

OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one.

The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face, causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation, or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development.

“Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.”

OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.”

That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

Back-to-back extreme rain events inundated the Four Corners region of the U.S. Southwest in late October and early November 2026. The storms alleviated short-term drought conditions in the Southwest but caused river levels to spike to record or near-record levels in places, triggering damaging floods. 

One effect of the heavy rains detected by satellites was the rapid rise of water levels in Navajo Reservoir. The change is visible in the images above, acquired on September 20 (left) and November 7 (right) with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9. In that time, the lake in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado rose by nearly 60 feet (18 meters), according to data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. (Note that the Bureau of Reclamation decreased releases from Navajo Dam on September 16 and 17.)

On November 7, the reservoir stood at its highest level since August 2019 and at 108 percent of the average capacity for that date. That contrasts with September 20, when it held just 60 percent of its average capacity. Due to snow drought across the West in winter 2025-26, the lake saw relatively little growth in the spring, when snowmelt often raises water levels.

The San Juan, Piedra, and other rivers swelled with runoff amid the wet weather. Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town along the San Juan River about 40 miles (64 kilometers) northeast of the lake, was especially hard-hit by flooding. In the first round of rain, 5.05 inches (12.8 centimeters) fell in the town, and on October 23 the river reached major flood stage. After more rain, the river spiked again on November 1, this time nearly to the record level set in 1911 during a devastating flood. Officials issued evacuation orders, and responders rescued dozens of people, according to news reports, while water inundated streets and damaged property.

Heavy rain and flooding have been widespread across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico in recent weeks. From early September through early November, precipitation totals were 2 to 4 times the average throughout the Four Corners region—an area beset by long-term drought that was exacerbated by snow drought and high temperatures in 2026.

Though the downpours posed hazards to communities along many rivers, they did provide drought relief throughout the region. Weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps, derived from a suite of satellite data products and ground-based observations, have indicated improvements to drought conditions due to the fall storms. The group’s November 3 summary noted that “short-term drought has ended for the Southwest and Great Basin,” although long-term drought persists in places.

Wet weather in the Southwest is often associated with El Niño events, when the segment of the jet stream flowing eastward near the equatorial Pacific tends to strengthen. Experts noted that the low-pressure system delivering the heavy rainfall in autumn 2026 was at a low latitude for the time of year and drew energy from unusually high ocean temperatures. El Niño patterns—like the one currently underway —can increase the likelihood of moisture-laden storms being steered across the Southwest interior.

articles.title: Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime
articles.description: New regulator will require modelmakers to test and allow inspection, but not much more
articles.content:
Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models.

Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks.

Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI.

That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.”

Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.”

The review suggests two ministries and Australia’s Federal Police consider those reforms, meaning this is not something that will happen in a hurry, if at all, for a couple of reasons.

One is that Australia yesterday proposed a new regulator which will require AI players to do six things:

Maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment

Identify and manage serious risks associated with their models

Allow independent evaluation of their models

Provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian Government rapidly

Maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency

Respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

If AI companies straighten up and fly right, Canberra might not need to do more.

The other reason Australia might not criminalize AI is economic pragmatism.

Canberra wants to ensure leading AI companies invest in local datacenters, especially facilities where they train and run frontier models. Such investments would mean Australia scores some of the AI boom cash sloshing around the world, while also giving the government the ability to at least point to leading-edge AI running on local shores and therefore theoretically remaining accessible even if war or a diplomatic rupture makes it hard to access advanced AI hosted offshore.

Other nations in Asia, such as South Korea and India, are addressing those risks by building substantial sovereign infrastructure and working to develop sovereign frontier-class models trained on local data and especially data in their local languages.

Canberra can’t match that investment without pouring petrol on its raging inflation problem. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is therefore instead trying to regulate AI without scaring away investment.

Threatening to lock up AI executives is not likely to make them enthusiastic when asked to approve building datacenters down under.

Some sections of Australia’s population won’t mind it if big tech doesn’t show up: Protests against datacenters are already widespread.

Your correspondent recently spoke to the organizer of a protest group opposed to development of a new datacenter which is just three kilometers from four existing bit barns, one of which abuts a sizable apartment complex and has operated without incident or opposition for years. The organizer was blissfully ignorant of those facilities and eventually said their group is opposed to AI in all forms. ®

articles.title: Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory
articles.description: Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data artifact types bring Claude closer to a productivity suite
articles.content:
Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google.

On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite.

Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications.

"An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains.

The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types –.txt,.md,.html,.jsx,.svg,.pptx,.docx,.zip,.pdf, and.mp4, among others.

Anthropic's vision of Claude as a container for other applications goes beyond artifacts. The AI biz has also expanded its interactive connectors, which turn Claude into a landlord for other software applications. Its own promotional video for the feature hammers that point home in its title: " Your apps have moved into Claude."

"Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs," Anthropic said. "Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses."

In a prior era, those would be fighting words. Tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have worked for years to maintain their positions as platform landlords. Anthropic's invitation to become a Claude tenant ought to set off competition alarm bells. But perhaps with LLMs being able to re-create other people's apps on demand, there's less interest in defending app boundaries as if they were moats to keep out rivals. With AI, the call is coming from inside the house.

Alongside the rollout of Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data, Anthropic is pushing the notion that Claude is useful for people working outside of computation and mathematics, the occupational category that, according to the company's own data, accounts for a larger share of Claude usage than any other.

"Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers," the biz insists, hauling out canned testimonials from the likes of Accenture and Datadog.

If Anthropic can demonstrate that there's an untapped market of non-coders who would welcome a Claude subscription, investors in the company's pending IPO will be glad to see it. ®

articles.title: Seagate's new hybrid drive raises some old questions
articles.description: The FireCuda Forge revisits an old idea, with some familiar questions.
articles.content:
Seagate doesn't think hybrid drives are done just yet. On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of the new FireCuda Forge line of storage drives. The new drives combine the high capacity of a traditional plattered HDD with the speed and responsiveness of a user-supplied solid-state drive (SSD). The new hybrid storage solution is Seagate's first to be powered and managed by the new Alkemi intelligent storage platform.

The FireCuda Forge is available right now through Seagate's web store, and comes in 8TB ($699) or 20TB ($899) HDD configurations—neither of which includes the required SSD. Users will have to bring their own SSD, with some specific restrictions. The FireCuda Forge is compatible with M.2 2280 NVMe drives that are PCIe Gen3 or higher. The maximum supported NVMe capacity is 1TB, which means that's as much data as you'll be able to dedicate to storage on the "fast side" of the hybrid setup. The NVMe will require minimum speeds of 2,400MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write, and a unit with DRAM cache is recommended. Seagate claims 2,500MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write speeds for the combined system, along with USB4 and support for Windows 11 and macOS 26+.

articles.content:
Amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices. But the company’s upcoming Ring Robotic products are also certain to intensify privacy concerns previously raised around a prior Amazon attempt to popularize a flying security camera.

The Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to plan patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture.

Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration.

articles.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
articles.description: Researcher finds 35,000 Grok Build apps wide open to anyone who looked for them.
articles.content:
Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.

The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.

You had one job

Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.
